Optik Art earrings

A pair of square earrings in white acrylic, screen-printed with nested black squares and rings, from Wendy Ramshaw and David Watkins’s Optik Art Jewellery.

Source
V&A: Earring, “Optik Art Jewellery”, T.338E&F-1982
Creator
Wendy Ramshaw and David Watkins (designers)
Made
1963–1965
Style
Op art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Mod, graphic, inexpensive
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected the V&A photograph of the pair T.338E&F-1982 (1600 × 1308 px), on black, in a scratchpad. No image is stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The V&A describes the pair as screen-printed acrylic (perspex) and base metal: an opaque white square with a screen-printed black op-art design. V&A.

The V&A’s record of a related ring says that Ramshaw and Watkins began Optik Art Jewellery in 1963, “inspired by Op-Art”. They screen-printed black and white patterns onto acrylic sheets and sliced the sheets into pieces, and Fenwicks of Bond Street commissioned collections. V&A.

Observed

  • Each earring is a flat square turned 45 degrees, with a black ground.
  • Inside, a white ring holds a black square on point, which holds a smaller white ring and a black square: circles and squares alternate inward.
  • Where a circle crosses a square, the white areas split into crescents and triangles, so figure and ground alternate.
  • The edges of the acrylic show as thin white lines.

Why it belongs

The earrings reduce op art to one emblem, much like Vasarely’s square-in-circle units, and make it a cheap fashion product.

Screen printing on a sheet and cutting it into pieces is the same industrial logic that made op prints easy to reproduce.

Borrow

Nest alternating circles and squares in black and white so that the crossings make crescents and triangles.

Turn a square badge or icon 45 degrees to give a static motif tension.
